items.title: FLUX 3 Image Klein
items.author: gmays
items.content:
Today we are releasing FLUX 3 Image Klein, a 5.6B parameter open weights model for text-to-image generation, image editing and multi-reference generation with up to 10 reference images. It shares core capabilities with the full FLUX 3 Image model: native 4K generation, pixel-perfect editing, and bounding boxes that control where elements are placed or confine edits to a defined area.

FLUX 3 Image Klein builds on FLUX 3's shared learnings across images, video and audio. Images contribute spatial detail, video adds motion and physical dynamics, and audio provides information about events and interactions. Together, these signals help the model generate images that feel grounded in the real world.

The release includes a base model for fine-tuning and a step distilled model for low-latency generation, along with FP8, INT8 and NVFP4 builds developed with NVIDIA support, under the FLUX Kommunity License.

Try it in the BFL API · Download the weights

Leading open weights quality with fewer parameters

In internal evaluations, FLUX 3 Image Klein ranks first in text-to-image, multi-reference generation and image editing, ahead of larger open weights models. It also rates above the closed models in the comparison, Ideogram V4.5 and FLUX.2 [pro]. At 5.6B parameters, it is the smallest open model in the comparison, against 7B for Qwen-Image 2.1 and 12.9B for Krea 2. Compared with FLUX.2 [klein] 9B, it gains 91 Elo in text-to-image and 70 in image editing, with 38% fewer parameters.

FLUX 3 Image Klein was also optimized for consumer GPUs. Fewer parameters make it practical to run locally and cheaper to adapt, and teams with data sovereignty or local deployment requirements can evaluate and adapt the model on their own infrastructure. This is also key for on-device image editing, allowing consumers to edit images directly on their favorite laptops. The generator weights require 11.2 GB in BF16 and 5.6 GB in FP8. With the INT8 build, FLUX 3 Image Klein runs on NVIDIA GeForce RTX GPUs with as little as 8GB of VRAM, through ComfyUI or Diffusers, extending what FLUX.2 [klein] started to even smaller hardware. With the distilled model and the INT8 build, it generates a 1MP image in about 4 seconds on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 and under 9 seconds on an RTX 4070 through ComfyUI.

The base checkpoint is built for fine-tuning: Diffusers and Ostris's AI Toolkit support LoRA training from day one, and NVIDIA's NeMo AutoModel ships recipes that work directly from the released checkpoints.

For even faster production workloads that need lower latency, we also work with teams on specific customizations that get you there. Get in touch.

On the speed–quality frontier

FLUX 3 Image Klein also extends the speed–quality Pareto frontier. Through the BFL API, it delivers lower latency than Qwen-Image 2.1, FLUX.2 [pro], Ideogram V4.5 and Krea 2, and the highest rating at its latency and above. In the charts below, the violet line traces the highest rating available at each latency and the gray line shows the previous frontier.

Latency is measured end to end, from request submission to the finished 1 MP image, including queueing. FLUX 3 Image Klein was timed on our servers. Other models were timed from the client, which includes polling and network time. Krea 2 was timed on its Medium tier; its Large tier took 31.1 seconds for text-to-image.

FLUX 3 Image Klein is available today as open weights and through the BFL API.

      The weights are available under the FLUX Kommunity License, which allows free commercial use for individuals and companies with annual revenue under $5M, alongside research and non-commercial use. Larger organizations can deploy commercially through our self-hosted licensing options or API.

      In an effort to make AI technology both open and safe, we implement multiple safeguards throughout the model development lifecycle to combat misuse. These include dataset filters during pre-training to limit exposure to harmful content, and targeted fine-tuning during post-training to suppress harmful behaviors, making it progressively harder to elicit harmful content. Ahead of the release, the FLUX 3 Image Klein checkpoints were rigorously red teamed internally and evaluated by our external safety partner Cinder, demonstrating substantially fewer vulnerabilities than other popular open weights models. More on our safety methodology is available here.

      FLUX 3 Image Klein is the second open weights release from the FLUX 3 family, following FLUX 3 Action. More will follow.

        If you use FLUX 3 Image Klein in your work, please cite:

        @misc{bfl2026flux3imageklein,
  author       = {{Black Forest Labs}},
  title        = {{FLUX} 3 Image Klein},
  year         = {2026},
  url          = {https://bfl.ai/blog/flux-3-image-klein},
}

items.title: eBay Restricts Listings of Radio Equipment, but Exempts Ham-Band-Only Gear
Designing more efficient quantum circuits with Claude
items.author: pretext
items.content:
Quantum computers will need carefully designed circuits to run useful algorithms on limited hardware. We gave Claude plain-language specifications for eight such circuits, drawn from chemistry, optimization, physics simulation, and number theory, along with an automated evaluator that checks and scores each design. Working largely on its own, Claude found designs that improve on the best published circuits, in some cases by an order of magnitude or more. Such improvements substantially reduce the quantum resources that useful applications require, so practical quantum computers could arrive sooner than previously anticipated.

This work was led by Andi Gu as part of Anthropic’s STEM Fellows Program, with mentorship from Alek Kemeny, a quantum physicist at Anthropic, in collaboration with Susanne Yelin (Harvard University) and Mikhail Lukin (Harvard University and QuEra Computing). Read the full paper on arXiv.

Unlike classical computers, which store information in bits whose value is either 0 or 1, quantum computers store information in which can be built from single atoms, superconducting circuits, or particles of light. These qubits make use of quantum phenomena such as —which allows a quantum system to exist in a combination of states at once—in order to process information in ways that could make certain problems in fields like chemistry, materials science, and number theory tractable, even when they are too hard for traditional computers.

The quantum computers the field has built to date only have hundreds to thousands of qubits—too few to run many of the algorithms that promise practical advantages over classical computers. And these qubits are highly sensitive to environmental noise, such as heat, vibration, and even cosmic rays. A tiny disturbance can nudge a qubit’s state, and these small errors pile up until the computer gives the wrong answer.

Given that both qubits and computing time are scarce resources, researchers have been working to redesign quantum algorithms to use fewer qubits and complete computations in less time. An illustrative example is simulating FeMoco, the iron–sulfur cluster at the heart of nitrogenase, the enzyme that bacteria use to turn nitrogen from the air into ammonia. Understanding how it works could help scientists design better industrial catalysts—the substances manufacturers use to speed up chemical reactions.

In 2017, researchers estimated that a quantum computer would need about 50 trillion Toffoli gates to compute FeMoco’s ground-state energy—the energy of its most stable configuration, which chemists need in order to predict how FeMoco reacts. (Similar to ordinary computers, quantum computers work by applying a long sequence of simple operations, called gates, to their qubits. The Toffoli gate is one of the most expensive gates to run, so counting Toffoli gates is a standard way to estimate how long a computation will take.)

Through a series of algorithmic advances, the estimated number of gates has come down to about 340 million—a roughly 150,000-fold reduction, corresponding to a few hours of computation on a future machine with about three million physical qubits.

These reductions largely came from redesigning the circuits that carry out the computation, rather than from making better hardware. Claude has proven particularly adept at optimizing classicalalgorithms, so we wanted to see whether it could do the same for quantum algorithms if it were given only a plain-language description of what each circuit must compute.

Claude is unusually well suited to this task, for several reasons. First, quantum algorithms are implemented as quantum . These are composed of sequences of gates, like the Toffoli gates mentioned above. Importantly, these circuits can be described in code, so we can make use of Claude’s coding capabilities to write, run, and revise circuit designs as ordinary programs. Second, the (fairly common) class of quantum algorithms we were most interested in optimizing can be tested efficiently for correctness, as each input gives one definite output that an ordinary computer can check. This means we could have an external evaluator program validate Claude’s proposals. Finally, we can give Claude a clear, objective score to improve: the number of qubits used, multiplied by the number of gates, which serves as a proxy for how long the circuit would take to run.

We found that Claude Mythos 5 could successfully work in a closed loop, proposing a circuit design, receiving feedback and a score from the evaluator program, and using that feedback to improve its next attempt, with no human input between rounds (see Figure 1). Across eight computational primitives—the basic routines that larger quantum algorithms are built from—for chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, number theory, and numerical computing, Claude discovered novel designs that used both fewer qubits and fewer gates than the best previously published algorithms (Figure 2). 

In each case, the improvement resulted from uncovering new structural and mathematical insights about the problem, rather than from fine-tuning existing designs. For example, when compiling a circuit for simulating an iron-sulfide molecule, Claude noticed that the molecule’s symmetries and repeating structure meant that some results could be calculated once and reused, rather than recomputed for every part of the system. In other cases, it found that existing circuits included costly components that were needed to handle only extremely rare inputs, and it redesigned them without those components.

Below, we describe two of Claude’s discoveries. The first is a new way to perform modular inversion, a bit of arithmetic that is the most expensive step in elliptic-curve calculations. The second makes the costliest step of a leading quantum optimization algorithm about 12x cheaper.

These results suggest that AI can now help redesign quantum circuits, a key step in making quantum algorithms faster and easier to run. Faster circuit design could bring the problems quantum computers are meant to solve—from designing new medicines and better batteries to finding cleaner ways of making fertilizer—within reach sooner.

A new reversible algorithm

Designing a quantum circuit involves two constraints that ordinary programming doesn’t have. The first is that a quantum circuit can’t make “if-then” decisions the way an ordinary program can. An ordinary program can check a value and then run only one of two pieces of code. But a quantum computer runs on a superposition of many inputs at once, some of which would run the first piece of code and some of which would run the second, so the circuit has to include the operations for both every time it runs. 

The second is that a quantum circuit can’t discard information. An ordinary program can overwrite or delete its scratch work once it’s completed it; in a quantum computer, such intermediate information can’t simply be erased, because every step of a quantum circuit must be reversible. Leaving that information in place isn’t an option, either, because leftover scratch work would corrupt the final result. The only way to discard information is to “uncompute” it by running the computation that created it in reverse, at the cost of additional gates. Both of these constraints make quantum circuits far more expensive, in both runtime and qubits, than their classical counterparts.

This constraint forces a difficult trade-off between space (i.e., qubits) and time. At one extreme, a quantum circuit can uncompute intermediate results as soon as they have been used. This frees up qubits, but if those same results are needed again later, the circuit must recompute them, which adds gates and increases the runtime. At the other extreme, the circuit can retain intermediate results until they’re no longer needed. This avoids repeating work, but it can require many more qubits.

This is what makes quantum circuit design an especially interesting test of Claude’s capabilities. The circuits can be written as ordinary code, but improving them requires the model to reason under a set of constraints quite unlike those of ordinary programming.

A hard first test: modular inversion

The first task we gave Claude was point addition, a rule for combining two points on a mathematical curve (an elliptic curve) to produce a third. Point addition is the core step in quantum algorithms for the discrete logarithm problem on elliptic curves: given a starting point and the result of adding it to itself times, find . For large curves, ordinary computers can’t solve this problem in any reasonable amount of time, but a sufficiently large quantum computer could.

These algorithms perform point addition many times over, including in reverse, and these additions account for most of their qubit and runtime costs. Problems like this—easy to compute, extremely hard to reverse—were among the first where quantum computers were shown to offer an exponential speedup over ordinary ones. For these reasons, point addition has become one of the field’s standard benchmarks. This made it a demanding test for Claude. So, we asked it to map out how few qubits, as well as how few gates, point addition really needs.

We gave Claude a one-paragraph brief. It explained the mathematical rule for point addition, and how the evaluator would check each proposed circuit for correctness and score it on the number of qubits and gates it used. It also instructed Claude to explore several approaches in parallel. After working for 53 hours with minimal human input (limited to the initial brief and occasional prompts to think more broadly), Claude arrived at a completely new approach to the problem.

The memory demands of divsteps

Most of the cost of point addition comes from a single step, called. Elliptic-curve arithmetic uses numbers that wrap back around when they reach a fixed limit. Modular inversion is the wraparound version of division: given an integer , find such that ≡ 1 (mod ). Ordinary computers can perform this operation efficiently using a method called . Divsteps starts with a pair of numbers and repeatedly simplifies them over many rounds of iteration. In each round, divsteps examines the current pair of numbers and conditionally swaps, adds, subtracts, or halves them. Along the way, it preserves just enough information to produce the modular inverse at the end.

Despite its success on ordinary computers, divsteps had not yet produced a practical quantum circuit, because of the reversibility constraint described above. The record of which operation was chosen at each iteration, called , is the kind of scratch work that a traditional program can simply discard. In contrast, a quantum circuit has to retain that record so the computation can be run backward. A straightforward quantum version of divsteps is therefore forced to accumulate a long history of branch information, which requires an enormous number of additional qubits to store.

How Claude got around the memory problem

Claude recognized that this divsteps approach could be promising for quantum circuits, but only if there were a way around needing to store the full history. It had an idea: perhaps the record didn’t need to be stored at all. Claude reasoned that it might be possible to directly infer (or “decode”) the branch information by carefully inspecting the pair of numbers after each iteration. In essence, the numbers themselves would store the record. The circuit could then be run backward without needing any extra qubits.

To test this idea, Claude explored a number of simple candidate rules for performing the decoding. These early rules worked on small test cases, but they failed when Claude tested them at the full problem size, on 256-bit numbers.

Claude then tried a more theoretical approach. Rather than guessing and testing rules, it set out to understand mathematically why divsteps behaves the way it does. It proved a series of results about the iteration process, including several new algebraic identities. From these identities, Claude derived a precise formula for the decoding rule that would correctly recover the branch information from the numerical pairs. It then checked the formula, first by running it through large-scale numerical simulations, and then formalizing the claim in Lean. With the full validation complete, Claude produced the first reversible implementation of divsteps with no stored branch history.

Decoding saves qubits, but it costs time. So, as a further refinement, Claude looked for situations in which it would be cheaper to store the branch information than to decode it. By varying the threshold at which the circuit stores rather than decodes the branch information, Claude produced a new family of designs between the two extremes. Compared with the smallest previous design, one circuit in the family uses 12% more qubits but 17x fewer gates. More generally, the new designs expand the Pareto frontier, offering combinations of qubit count and runtime that weren’t available before (Table 1).

Optimizing a quantum optimizer

Optimization problems are at the heart of a wide range of tasks, including scheduling, logistics, and materials design. An optimization problem presents a set of competing constraints and asks for the solution that satisfies as many of them as possible. Many quantum algorithms have been proposed for problems like these, but most promise only modest or uncertain gains over ordinary computers. Decoded quantum interferometry (DQI) is one of the strongest candidates for offering a superpolynomial quantum speedup—an advantage that rapidly widens as the problems get larger.

When a quantum computer finishes a computation, reading out its qubits produces just one answer, selected at random from the possibilities they were holding in superposition. DQI works by preparing a quantum state in which good solutions are more likely to be read out than bad ones. Doing this involves using an error-correcting decoder, which recovers a short list of “errors” from a compact summary. This is the most expensive step in the algorithm. So, if we could make a faster decoder, we could also perform DQI faster.

A more efficient quantum decoder

The researchers who introduced DQI demonstrated it on a problem called optimal polynomial intersection (OPI), a grid-based version of curve fitting (Figure 3). Imagine a grid in which each position contains several acceptable values of . The goal is to find a simple curve (a low-degree polynomial) that passes through an acceptable square for as many positions as possible. DQI tackles this optimization problem using a specific type of decoder, called a Reed-Solomon decoder.

Reed-Solomon decoding starts from the compact summary of errors mentioned above, which is known as a . The decoder’s job is to infer, from this summary, where in the data the errors occurred and what they were. The previous state-of-the-art quantum circuit processed these syndromes using the extended Euclidean algorithm, a sequence of divisions and swaps in which the number and order of steps depend on the particular input it’s given. Here, the constraints of quantum circuits reemerge: while an ordinary program can follow a different path for every input, a quantum circuit, working on many inputs at once, has to handle all of them with a single fixed sequence of gates. To manage this, the previous design had to stretch the computation over many more rounds of iteration than any single input would need, and had to run every operation in every round, even when doing so was unnecessary.

Improving this decoder could substantially reduce DQI’s runtime. Estimates by researchers at Google Quantum AI imply that solving one particular OPI problem would take about three months on Frontier, one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers, compared with roughly an hour on a future quantum computer running DQI. Most of that hour would be spent on Reed-Solomon decoding.

So, we asked Claude to design a more efficient quantum circuit for the decoding step. Claude quickly concluded that the extended Euclidean algorithm was a poor fit for a quantum circuit. Instead, it organized its circuit around a different decoding method, known as Berlekamp-Massey decoding, which reads through syndromes (summaries of errors) one at a time and gradually works out the simplest rule that predicts each number in the list based on the ones that came before it. Once that rule is found, it reveals the errors. Unlike the extended Euclidean algorithm, Berlekamp-Massey performs the same kind of step in every round and always runs the same number of rounds, which suits a quantum circuit’s single fixed sequence of gates, ultimately giving Claude a much more efficient foundation to build on.

A simplified approach to storage

Switching to Berlekamp-Massey removed the need for the circuit to take different paths for different inputs. But making it reversible introduced another challenge, this time as a result of the uncomputing constraint discussed above. In every round, the circuit calculates temporary values that it needs only briefly, but this information can’t simply be deleted: to uncompute it later, the circuit has to be able to recover that information.

Storing this information would have been prohibitively expensive. So Claude took the same kind of approach as it had for divsteps: it found a way to reconstruct most of this information from the circuit’s current state, so it didn’t need to be stored. However, a few exceptional values couldn’t be recovered in this way and had to be saved.

Setting aside enough memory for the worst possible case, in which an exceptional value arises in 35 different rounds, would take 665 qubits. Instead, Claude wrote a high-speed simulator and ran 403 million sample decodings to measure how often these exceptions actually occurred. Almost every run needed to save one value at most. So Claude’s circuit sets aside room for just one saved value, or 19 qubits. About one run in 10,000 needs more than that and fails, which is well within the error rate the task allows. These improvements replaced large, worst-case reserves with a small, fixed number of qubits and gates (Figure 4).

Together, these optimizations reduced the number of gates in the decoder by a factor of 12 relative to Google’s previous construction. The improvement came from redesigning the computation at three levels: a different method (replacing the extended Euclidean algorithm with Berlekamp-Massey decoding), a different circuit architecture (reconstructing temporary values instead of storing them), and a different resource budget (measuring precisely how much memory and computation the circuit really needed). No single change would have been enough on its own, but together, they make the most expensive step of DQI just a little over an order of magnitude cheaper.

Scientific progress often comes from making theoretical ideas practical. One of the main ways this happens is by making a process that was once thought to be impractical fast and cheap enough to carry out. Quantum circuit design is a prime example: the 150,000-fold drop in the FeMoco estimate described above took many research groups eight years, with each step typically representing months of work. By contrast, Claude’s elliptic-curve design was the result of a single 53-hour run.

Our results suggest that AI can support the work of circuit design, producing implementations that bring useful quantum computations closer to the capabilities of real hardware. If AI can speed up that work, useful quantum computing could arrive sooner.

Despite Claude’s encouraging performance on these tasks, we also observed some limitations. In our early experiments, Claude was conservative by nature. It repeatedly second-guessed apparent improvements, and sometimes continued to double- and even triple-check results that were already well supported. This caution was sometimes valuable: for example, it prompted Claude to write Lean proofs to verify its divsteps design. But it also manifested in a tendency to prefer existing, well-known approaches to more novel ones. 

We took two steps to mitigate this. First, our setup required Claude to propose several qualitatively different approaches, and to develop them in parallel. Second, we also occasionally prompted Claude to broaden its search. These interventions succeeded in getting Claude to pursue more ambitious ideas. The elliptic-curve result, for example, didn’t come from shaving gates off of a pre-existing design but from exploring a method of doing reversible modular inversion that hadn’t been possible previously, and then deriving the mathematical results needed to make it practical. Once it had come up with the idea, Claude developed the approach, implemented it, and verified its correctness autonomously.

Circuit design is only one part of building a useful quantum computer. Because qubits are so fragile, the machine must also catch and fix its own errors as it runs, and that depends on many other components, ranging from error-correcting codes to fast decoders to control of the hardware itself. These components all affect one another, but to manage complexity, each is usually designed separately. Many of them share the characteristics that made circuit design a good fit for Claude: a design can be written as code, checked for correctness, and scored by its cost. 

This raises an intriguing possibility. Rather than designing each component on its own, AI could optimize all of them jointly, from the algorithm down to the hardware, to build an entire error-corrected quantum computer tailored to a specific problem. Such designs could also tell hardware builders which capabilities matter most for a given application. That could put problems such as designing catalysts and understanding new materials within reach of the first fault-tolerant machines.

We thank Arjun Kar and Vinay Ramasesh for helpful discussions in the early stages of the project.

items.title: I built the RealWorld app in Lean 4
items.author: saviorand
items.content:
Lean 4 is a functional programming language in the same family as Haskell and OCaml. Most people know it as a proof assistant. Lately its standard library has also gained an HTTP server. The community is writing the other libraries that ordinary apps need too, like Postgres drivers, cryptography and HTML rendering.

So can you build a real web app in Lean yet? I built RealWorld in it to find out. RealWorld is a well-known reference app, a Medium clone that comes with official test suites for its API and its website. My version is written entirely in Lean including the frontend, which uses datastar-lean for interactivity. The code is on GitHub.

I’ve written this post like a math paper, mostly because it’s fun and partly because it keeps the structure clear. Most of what follows is still plain engineering of the kind you would do in any language. The few things that are actually proved are marked as propositions. Lean checks those proofs every time the code builds.

The first question is whether a RealWorld app can be built in Lean at all. The test suites turn that into something we can check.

. A is a program that passes RealWorld’s API suite and its website suite.

. There is a RealWorld implementation in Lean.

The proof is to build one. The test suites define what it has to do. The API tests send HTTP requests and check the JSON that comes back, so we need a server. The data in those answers has to be kept between requests, which means a database. The website tests click through the site in a real browser, so the server has to render pages as well.

(The server). Lean’s standard library has had an HTTP server, , since April. It takes care of all the low-level connection handling for you. On top of that server I use lean-routing to declare the API’s routes in a table. Each route has a path with typed parameters and gets its own handler. Read in the code below as :

  [ ...
    comment := ,
    ... ]

 (env : ) (slug : ) (id : ) :  :=  req => respond 
  Service.deleteComment env (← requireUser env req) slug id
  noContent

 (env : ) :  () :=
  [ ...
    .delete patterns.comment (deleteComment env),
    ... ]

This handler deletes a comment. It checks the user’s login token with , calls the service layer to delete the comment and replies with . The website calls the same service layer and therefore follows exactly the same rules. Everything else comes from libraries, as it would in any language:

(The database). The data lives in Postgres. I talk to it through leanpostgres, which wraps Postgres’s C client and keeps a pool of connections. You write the SQL right in the code. Each row that comes back is turned into a Lean structure:

 (db : ) (email : ) :  () := 
  first (← db sql!)

The inside becomes a query parameter, which Postgres receives separately from the SQL text. So user input can never run as SQL. The database schema is plain SQL that leanmigrate applies when the server starts.

(The website). The pages are rendered on the server with lean-html. There are no templates because the HTML is written as ordinary Lean functions. This one shows a comment, plus a trash icon if you wrote it:

 (viewer : ) (slug : ) (c : ) :  .flow :=
   delete :  ( .phrasing) :=
     viewer.any (·.id == c.authorId) 
      [ span [ i [] { class_ :=  } ] { class_ :=  }
          [onClick (action  (Site.links.comment slug c.id.toInt.toNat))] ]
     []
  div [
    div [ p [ c.body ] { class_ :=  } ] { class_ :=  },
    ...
  ] { class_ := , id := s! }

That is all the frontend code needed to delete a comment. Datastar, a small script on the page, sends the request when you click the icon. It then updates the page with the server’s reply. The server builds that reply with the same function the JSON API uses. There’s no frontend build step because the pages are just HTML plus one script. On the server I use datastar-lean, the official Lean SDK for Datastar that Carlo Hamalainen and I maintain.

Put the three parts together and run both test suites against the result. They pass.

(On cost). The Lean backend comes to 1,033 lines, the shortest of the four implementations I compared. The TypeScript one has 1,267 lines, the Go one 1,371 and the C# one 2,396. Ten of the eleven libraries it uses are by Paul Butcher. Claude Code and I contributed fixes to six of them along the way.

Passing tests on a laptop doesn’t mean an app is ready for real users. So the second question is about production.

. Can the implementation of Theorem 1 serve real users?

(A young stack). Lean’s HTTP server maxes out at a few thousand requests per second per process. That’s mostly due to a bug in Lean’s runtime, which is already fixed but not yet released. Lean also ships a new version every month. New versions often break libraries. Neither problem matters for a small site that pins its versions.

(Who wrote it). Almost none of this code was written by hand. Claude Code wrote the app at my direction. Most of the libraries were written the same way. It’s all a few months old. Most of it has only one or two contributors. Code written this fast hasn’t had many readers or users yet. So the kind of bugs you only find in real use are probably still in there.

The easiest parts to trust are the types and the theorems, because Lean checks them. Those hold no matter who or what wrote the code. The instructions the libraries give their AI agent push in this direction. They ask for “the strongest form a claim admits: a proven theorem over a property … over an example and an expected result”. They also forbid using as a placeholder for a missing proof. Several of the libraries do include real proofs. Code that no theorem covers is only as reliable as its tests. That goes double for the bindings to C libraries, where Lean can’t check the C code at all.

You still need to read the proved parts, though. Lean checks that each proof is correct, but it can’t check whether the theorem states what you actually need. Agents asked for proofs often prove things that don’t matter. When Dan Luu had coding agents implement Zstd compression and told them to use Lean 4, they mostly proved arithmetic facts that missed the bug-prone code. Those proofs didn’t make the code any more correct. So you still have to read all of it, theorems and proofs included. Check that it does what you need and fix it where it doesn’t. Don’t trust any part you haven’t checked yourself.

Tools like claimcheck can help with that reading. It has an AI model restate each theorem in plain English without knowing what the theorem was meant to say. A second step compares that restatement with the original intent. It’s a useful check, but it doesn’t replace reading.

Partial answer to Question 2. So can the app serve real users? Yes, as long as three things hold: (H1) traffic stays modest, (H2) you pin the toolchain, and (H3) someone actually reads the code. The server’s limits don’t matter while traffic stays modest. You can also run several copies of the app for more load because it keeps no state between requests. A pinned toolchain means a new Lean release can’t break anything until you choose to upgrade. Reading the code is doable where it matters most because the app is only about 1,600 lines. Someone should read its handlers, its SQL and its C bindings carefully before real users see them.

I think correctness by construction is what you should aim for, especially when an AI writes most of your code. It means first writing down exactly what the program should do in a formal language. The code is then derived from that description in steps that are each proved correct.

Today most people rely on tests instead, or hand the agent a spec and hope it follows it. Tests only check the cases someone thought to write. Dan Luu’s experiments also show that agents write poor tests, even when told which technique to use. A spec on its own can’t show that the code actually follows it. Correctness by construction closes that gap, because Lean checks every step from the spec to the code. It’s the only reliable way I see to ship high-quality code while keeping the speed AI gives you.

So the last question is whether this app could be correct by construction. Here is the precise definition.

. A program is if it is derived from a formal specification by steps, each proved to preserve correctness.

. Is there a RealWorld implementation in Lean that is correct by construction?

Definition 2 has two parts, a formal specification and a step-by-step derivation from it. Let’s check each one.

Does RealWorld have a formal specification? Partly. Its contract is an OpenAPI file plus the test suites. The OpenAPI file is precise about shapes, like which endpoints exist, what fields they take and which status codes they return. What the endpoints actually do is only described in English. The tests pin that down for the specific cases they check, and nowhere else. So RealWorld is formal about types and informal about behavior.

Was the app derived from that specification? No. That was a conscious choice. RealWorld is only formal about types, so there’s nothing precise enough to derive the app’s behavior from. Full correctness by construction wasn’t possible with the spec as it stands. So I wrote the app first and tested it afterwards, which is the opposite of what Definition 2 asks for. I picked a few important properties to verify instead. Three of them are guaranteed just because the code compiles. Here they are.

. If a handler’s types don’t match its route, the code doesn’t compile.

lean-routing works out each handler’s type from its route. The OpenAPI file says a comment’s id is an integer. The route table says as well. So a handler that takes the id as a won’t compile:

error: Application type mismatch: The argument
  deleteComment env
has type
  String → String → Api.Handler
but is expected to have type
  HandlerType Api.patterns.comment Result

This error appears at compile time, before the app ever runs.

Every handler in Express or Go parses the id itself. A mismatch in Rust’s axum only shows up when a request comes in. One weak spot remains here. I copied the route table from the OpenAPI file by hand. Generating it from the file automatically would close that gap.

Slugs show Definition 2 on a small scale. A slug is the URL-friendly version of a title, like . RealWorld doesn’t say what a slug should look like, so I wrote the specification first, as a Lean type called . A single lowercase letter or digit is a valid slug. You can grow a valid slug by putting a letter or digit in front of it, or a letter or digit followed by a hyphen. Nothing else is valid. That rules out empty slugs, hyphens at either end and double hyphens. A is a string bundled with a proof that it follows these rules:

 :  → 
  | single {c} : isSlugChar c →  [c]
  | cons {c rest} : isSlugChar c →  rest →  (c :: rest)
  | hyphen {c rest} : isSlugChar c →  rest →  (c :: '-' :: rest)


  toString : 
  valid :  toString.toList

. Every slug the app stores is well formed.

The functions that save slugs only accept a , so every saved slug carries its proof. Most of those proofs come from when it turns a title into a slug. It only compiles because it comes with a proof that its result is valid for every possible title.

Here’s . It calls a helper, , which keeps the title’s letters and digits, lowercases them and turns everything in between into single hyphens. Then returns that string together with a proof that it’s valid. The proof is the part after :

 (title : ) :  :=
   h : chars title.toList false false 
  | [] => ⟨, ...⟩   
  | c :: cs =>
    ⟨String.ofList (c :: cs), 
      rw [String.toList_ofList, ← h]
      exact (chars_valid title.toList false).resolve_left ( rw [h]; exact List.cons_ne_nil _ _)⟩

That proof relies on a lemma about . It says that for any title, returns either nothing or a valid slug. The lemma is proved by induction over the title’s characters:

 (cs : ) (pending : ) :
    chars cs false pending = [] ∨  (chars cs false pending) := 
  induction cs generalizing pending 
  | nil => exact Or.inl rfl
  | cons c cs ih => ...

In total that’s about forty lines of proof for ten lines of code. A property-based test would check a few thousand random titles. The proof covers every title including the ones nobody has written yet.

. Unless the code calls , anything a user typed is escaped before it appears on a page.

You can’t build a page element in lean-html directly. Only lean-html’s own functions can. All of them except run their text through . lean-html also proves that never leaves a , or in its output:

 (c : ) :  :=
   c 
  | '&' => 
  | '<' => 
  | '>' => 
  | '"' => 
  | c    => String.singleton c

 (s : ) :
    ∀ c ∈ (escape s).toList, c ≠ '<' ∧ c ≠ '>' ∧ c ≠ '"' := ...

In plain words, the escaped version of any string contains no , or .

RealWorld’s website tests do check for cross-site scripting. They inject malicious text through the API and check that the page shows it as plain text. The suite skips those tests for apps that serve both the API and the pages, like this one. So here the proof is the only check. React escapes text the same way, but there only tests check that the escaping is right.

So this app is not correct by construction. Whether any RealWorld app in Lean can be (Question 3) is still open. Answering it would start with writing RealWorld’s behavior down in Lean. Deriving the app from that would also need a model of SQL, plus proofs about the C libraries and underneath. For now, the slug is the only part where the method has been carried all the way through.

Instructions for running the app and both test suites are in the repository.

Thanks to Paul Butcher, whose libraries made this possible, and to Carlo Hamalainen for datastar-lean.

items.title: Monte-Carlo Simulations
items.author: ibobev
items.content:
Monte Carlo simulations (or ) is the technique of applying randomness and the Law of large numbers to the solution of various scientific and engineering problems. One of its first documented uses was by Stanislaw Ulam and John von Neumann for nuclear weapon simulations after WWII .

In this post I want to provide examples of some simple uses of Monte Carlo simulations. We'll start with the classical example of calculating the value of by throwing darts.

Suppose we take a square board and inscribe a quarter of a circle into it. We then proceed to throw darts at the board and record whether each dart hits inside or outside the quarter circle. Having thrown many such darts, we calculate the ratio of the darts inside the circle to the total number thrown.

Assuming our darts are distributed uniformly over the square, by the Law of large numbers this ratio should approach the ratio of areas of the quarter circle to the full square .

With a square side length of 1, we have:

Change the number of samples (dart throws) and click "Run" to regenerate. The code is very simple - here's a slightly sanitized version:

You'll notice that the estimate is relatively poor - even with 1000 samples - if
you click "Run" several times, some numbers will be way off mark. While this
method does estimate , it's not a particularly  estimate. I
find that running ~10 billion samples is necessary to estimate it to 4 digits
after the decimal with reasonable reliability.
In general, for independent trials like these, the typical sampling error
decreases in proportion to , where N is the number of trials.
This means that halving the error requires four times as many samples.
While the  estimation may seem whimsical, it's an example of an
important class of problems to which Monte Carlo simulation is applied:
numerical integration. Our simulation estimates the area
under the quarter-circle curve, which is a definite integral.
Many integrals are very difficult to solve analytically, and much research has
been done in the area of numerical analysis to develop methods to calculate
integrals. Monte Carlo methods are
particularly useful for high-dimensional integrals, where other numerical
methods can become prohibitively expensive.
Combinatorial simulation - the game of SET
A common use of Monte Carlo methods is estimating complex combinatorial
calculations. These often don't have analytical solutions, and enumerating all
options is intractable due to the scale of the numbers involved. As an example,
let's consider the game of SET. Each SET card has four
attributes:
  1. Number of shapes (1, 2 or 3)
  2. Color (Red, Green or Purple)
  3. Shape type (Oval, Diamond or Squiggle)
  4. Shading (Empty, Striped or Solid)
And the goal is to find a "set" - three cards that are either all different or
all the same for each attribute separately. As an example, here's
a hand with a single set; see if you can find it :
And the next hand doesn't have any sets:
Here's a question: given a freshly shuffled SET deck, what are the odds that
the first 12 cards drawn will have no sets among them? This question is
difficult to answer without using a computer.
It's easy to calculate the number of ways to deal a 12-card hand from
a deck of 81:
But how many of these hands have no sets? Enumerating 70 trillion SET hands
and checking each one can take quite a while, and there is no straightforward
counting formula to answer this question. Some clever methods can be employed to
leverage symmetries and other mathematical properties of SET to cut down this
search space considerably. Donald Knuth himself worked on this problem and came
up with a neat program ( on his programs page) that found 2,284,535,476,080
such hands. Therefore, the answer to our question is:
There's a 3.23% chance that a randomly drawn hand of 12 cards from a full deck
of SET will have no set in it.
Let's see how we can use a Monte Carlo simulation to answer this question
with relatively small effort, without deep knowledge of the mathematical
properties of SET that enable cutting down the search space Knuth-style.
We can use the following pseudo-code:
C = 0
run N times:
  draw a random 12-card hand from a fresh deck
  count sets in the hand
  if no sets:
    C += 1

Estimated probability = C / N

After running 10 million simulated draws, I got an answer of 0.0323, which
matches the real answer very closely.
The Monte Carlo approach lets us solve rather complicated problems in a very
simple way. Suppose we want to answer the same question for a hand of 15 cards;
this would blow up the search space considerably - there are about 100x more
ways to select 15-card hands than there are to select 12-card hands. But for
a Monte Carlo simulation, we adjust one small parameter and get a very reliable
 answer (about 0.00037, in case you were wondering).
One domain where Monte Carlo simulations are ubiquitous is projections for
retirement portfolios. Suppose someone prepares to retire with a total sum
of 1 million dollars in their portfolio; they'd like to be able to draw
$30,000 a year from the portfolio for their living expenses. Would that work?
There's a large number of factors to take into account when analyzing this
question, but for simplicity let's focus on just two: portfolio return and
inflation. We can run a naive estimate, assuming average values: suppose an
average yearly portfolio return of 4%, and average yearly inflation of 2% 
Let's denote our portfolio return as , and inflation as
. Then the real return each year is:
Starting with $1,000,000, at the end of the year we'll have $1,019,600
and then draw $30,000 for living expenses , ending with $989,600. If we
continue this way, the money runs out after ~55 years, which means that a
person retiring at the age of 65 should be reasonably safe, right?
But this is ; assuming just average returns is risky, because
they do a poor job of representing reality, and many factors have uncertainty.
For example, the sequence of returns matters a lot; a bad year (-10%) followed
by a great year (+18%) would still count as "4% on average" but produces
significantly less money than two consecutive +4% years.
Inflation is also unpredictable, and sometimes
correlated with portfolio returns; there could be bad years of high inflation and
low / volatile returns that can wreak havoc on a portfolio.
As we add factors (variance in yearly draws, mixed portfolios of stocks, bonds,
real estate, life expectancy, unexpected events, changing tax laws etc.),
relying on a single average estimate becomes increasingly more fraught. This
is why Monte Carlo simulations are very popular in this domain: by drawing
from reasonable distributions based on historical data, a Monte Carlo simulation
can easily run a million different scenarios and provide estimates: for example,
what are the odds of money running out before death.
Here's a useful chart from a simulation I ran:
  • The dashed line shows the constant assumptions mentioned before: what happens
when yearly return is always 4% and inflation is always 2%.
  • The shaded blue areas demonstrate the outcomes of 1,000,000 simulations where
inflation and return numbers are drawn from reasonable normal distributions
based on historical data. We see that in 25% of the cases, all money ran out
by roughly 22 years.
  • It's even easier to see how long the funds last; if we're interested in
knowing, say, what are the odds that this plan will have enough money for
30 years - the chart shows it's about 60% (since in 40% of the simulations
the funds were depleted at this point).
Looking a this simulation, under the current assumptions the plan sounds much
riskier than the average assumption makes it appear. Assuming that a 65-y.o.
person would plan for
25 years of retirement until death, the ~30% odds of not having sufficient funds
for this duration of time are sobering. Perhaps a change in plans is needed
(such as a more frugal lifestyle or securing additional funds in some way).
Retirement projection is only one of may ways in which Monte Carlo simulations
are used for financial and economical applications; given the high uncertainty
of these domains, it's very difficult to plan using analytical calculations.
Company sales projections, growth projections, stock offering prices and much
more uses Monte Carlo simulations to arrive at estimates with reasonable error
bars.
